teaser: The title is polite. Nothing else in the picture is.
review_notes:
Bellows's original title used a racial slur naming a Black and a white fighter; I describe it without quoting it. Check wording preferred by the app.
Public prizefighting banned in New York State in 1909 and the one-night 'membership' workaround: standard account, check.
Jack Johnson won the heavyweight title on December 26, 1908; Johnson v. Jeffries on July 4, 1910.
Painting dated October 1909; dimensions about 115 x 160 cm; NGA Chester Dale Collection.
Comparison with Goya is a common art-historical reading, not a documented statement by Bellows.

lesson.text: Read the title, then look at the picture. “Both Members of This Club” sounds like a line from a dinner speech, two gentlemen being introduced. What you see is a man with blood on his face about to go down, and a crowd howling for it. The words and the image pull in opposite directions, and George Bellows meant them to.

The title quotes the ring announcer. In 1909 public prizefighting was banned in New York State. Private clubs were a loophole: if a boxer was made a “member” for the night, the bout became a private entertainment among members. Before each fight the announcer presented the two men that way.

So the phrase was already a small lie when it was spoken. Bellows adds a second, sharper one. One fighter is white, one is Black. In 1909 no real club in New York would have welcomed them both through its front door. Here, for one evening, they are equals by legal fiction.
Bellows first gave the canvas a blunter title that named the two men by race, using a slur for the Black fighter. He changed it before the picture was exhibited.

He painted it in October 1909, two months after “Stag at Sharkey's”, on a bigger canvas: about 115 by 160 centimeters (45 by 63 inches). The timing matters. Ten months earlier Jack Johnson had become the first Black heavyweight champion of the world, and much of white America was loudly demanding a challenger to take the title back.
With that in mind, see which way the force runs in this picture, and who is winning. Bellows builds the answer out of two long lines, one for each body, and a third that stays still.

lines.label: The drive
lines.text: The Black fighter's body is one long diagonal, from his back foot at the lower right through his shoulder to the gloves at the top. Everything in him pushes up and to the left.

lines.label: The buckle
lines.text: The white fighter is nearly vertical, but the line bends: knee dropping, torso arched back, head thrown up. He is absorbing the push and starting to fold.

lines.label: The rope
lines.text: A pale rope crosses behind them at shoulder height. It is the only straight, steady thing in the ring.

lesson.text: The winner is the Black boxer, and Bellows hides nothing about it. But notice where the light falls. The white fighter is lit like a figure on a stage, pale chest, green trunks, a face that is one smear of red. His opponent is painted in deep browns and stays half inside the darkness, powerful and almost faceless.
Neither man is the ugliest thing in the room. For that you have to look down, below the ropes, at the people who paid to watch and are getting what they came for.

lesson.title: The members
lesson.text: Below the ropes, the crowd. Bellows saves his cruelest brushwork for them.

spots.title: The loser's face
spots.text: No eyes, no mouth you can read. The head is a patch of red and pink tipped back under his own raised arms. Bellows paints the damage and leaves out the person.

spots.title: The grin
spots.text: A wide open mouth full of teeth, a face lit gray from above. He is delighted. Faces like this owe a debt to Goya, the Spanish painter of mobs and nightmares.

spots.title: The shouter
spots.text: At the far left a red-faced man leans over the rope with his arm stretched toward the ring, urging the fight on.

spots.title: Faces in the dark
spots.text: On the right, heads float up out of the black like lanterns. Each is a few strokes: a brow, a cheek, an open mouth.

lesson.text: The fighters are painted as bodies under strain. The spectators are painted as appetites. Bellows turns the question of who is savage back onto the audience, and you are standing in it.

On July 4, 1910, Jack Johnson defended his title against the former champion Jim Jeffries, who had been talked out of retirement to beat him. Johnson won. Riots followed in cities across the United States.

Bellows never said what he thought about any of this. He left a title that calls two men equal, a painting that shows one of them winning, and a crowd that enjoys both facts for the wrong reasons. Which of the three is the subject?

quiz.question: Where does the title come from?
options: The announcer's words introducing the fighters
quiz.explanation: Boxers were presented as club members to get around the ban on public fights.

quiz.question: Which fighter is dominating the bout?
options: The Black fighter driving in from the right
The white fighter on the left
quiz.explanation: His body forms a long diagonal pushing the other man back.

quiz.question: Who had become heavyweight champion shortly before the painting was made?
quiz.explanation: Johnson won the title in December 1908, ten months before the picture.

quiz.question: How does Bellows treat the spectators?
quiz.explanation: The crowd is painted with harsh, grotesque faces.

quiz.question: Why were fighters made club “members” for a night?
options: Because public prizefights were banned in New York
quiz.explanation: A private bout between members slipped through the law.

facts.text: This canvas is smaller than “Stag at Sharkey's”.
facts.explanation: It is larger, about 115 by 160 centimeters.

facts.text: The white fighter is the most brightly lit figure in the picture.
facts.explanation: His pale body catches the light while his opponent stays in deep browns.

facts.text: Bellows kept the first title he gave the painting.
facts.explanation: He replaced a blunter, racially explicit title before exhibiting it.
